tier_reason: The README Performance section lists first-party single-node, RF=1 numbers (~241K msgs/sec with 4 publishers and pub-batch=100) and states that NATS JetStream reaches ~220K msgs/sec 'with similar settings'. The bench/producer and bench/consumer tools are public, but no hardware, OS, Go version or message size is tied to the table. The JetStream figure has no source, code or run configuration, so this stays at C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: ~241K msgs/sec (4 publishers, pub-batch=100, single node, RF=1) vs NATS JetStream's ~220K msgs/sec, which the README quotes 'with similar settings (pubbatch=100, file storage, RF=1)' - about 1.1x higher throughput (derived from page data)
corrections.workload: Single-node Liftbridge with replication factor 1, 4 concurrent publishers and pub-batch=100. The README's Running Benchmarks section shows the repo's bench/producer tool with 256-byte messages and ack-policy leader, but the table does not state which size or ack policy it used. 'File storage' is stated only for the JetStream side.
corrections.caveats: Self-reported numbers with no hardware, CPU model, OS or Go version for either side. The ~220K msgs/sec JetStream figure has no source, version, benchmark code or run configuration in the repo; the settings are only called 'similar', so this is not a side-by-side run. The ~1.1x margin is small enough to be within run-to-run variation. The same commit (bd763768, 2026-01-06) that added the numbers also added an RF=1 fast path that skips the commit queue under LEADER/NONE ack policies. The headline therefore reflects a single-node, leader-ack setup rather than durable replicated throughput. Liftbridge also requires a NATS server underneath.

tier_reason: The README's embedded chart (1 KiB cross-process ping-pong on x86 Linux) shows msgq at 362.13k and pyzmq at 113.97k messages/sec, alongside zenoh 86.03k, LCM 173.68k and multiprocessing.Pipe 231.66k. The benchmark code (msgq/examples/benchmark.py) is public, but no CPU model, compiler or flags are given, so it is first-party C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: 362.13k msgs/sec (msgq) vs 113.97k msgs/sec (pyzmq ZeroMQ IPC), 1 KiB cross-process ping-pong on x86 Linux - about 3.2x higher (derived from page data; the figures are read from the bar chart embedded in the README)
corrections.workload: 1 KiB cross-process ping-pong on x86 Linux. Messages/sec counts both requests and replies and is the median of 5 randomized repeats, each at least 2 s and 1000 round trips. The comparison covers msgq, pyzmq IPC (XPUB/SUB over ipc://), multiprocessing.Pipe, Eclipse Zenoh (unix socket) and LCM UDP, all driven from Python by the repo's msgq/examples/benchmark.py.
corrections.caveats: The README states only 'x86 Linux': no CPU model, kernel, compiler or flags. Both sides are driven through Python bindings (msgq's own binding vs pyzmq), not native C++ ZeroMQ. The test is synchronous ping-pong, so the rate is set by round-trip latency rather than streaming throughput. msgq uses a shared-memory ring buffer, while pyzmq goes over ipc:// Unix-domain sockets. The script also measures 64 B and 64 KiB messages, but only the 1 KiB results are plotted and published.
